text: In nineteenth-century Japanese kimono dressing, excess garment length can be drawn up beneath the obi sash. A straight-seamed robe is adjusted by wrapping and folding rather than requiring a new fitted cut for each wearer.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; Victoria and Albert Museum, Kimono; https://www.vam.ac.uk/articles/kimono . Facts paraphrased; no museum prose or images reproduced.

text: The V&A’s historical Japanese kimono account distinguishes unlined summer robes from robes with multiple winter linings. The same basic garment shape accommodates different seasons by changing its layers.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; Victoria and Albert Museum, Kimono; https://www.vam.ac.uk/articles/kimono . Facts paraphrased; no museum prose or images reproduced.

text: On historical Japanese kimono, pine, bamboo, and plum form the Three Friends of Winter motif, associated with longevity, perseverance, and renewal. Plum blossoms on a winter robe can anticipate the coming spring.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; Victoria and Albert Museum, Kimono; https://www.vam.ac.uk/articles/kimono . Facts paraphrased; no museum prose or images reproduced.

text: Historical Japanese kimono can allude to stories without depicting their characters: dropped fans may suggest interrupted lovers. Objects and landscape details carry the narrative while human figures remain comparatively unusual in the decoration.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; Victoria and Albert Museum, Kimono; https://www.vam.ac.uk/articles/kimono . Facts paraphrased; no museum prose or images reproduced.

text: Early twentieth-century Japanese boys’ kimono increasingly depicted trains, cars, aircraft, and skyscrapers. The V&A notes that such imagery expressed modernity and became more militaristic in the 1930s.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; Victoria and Albert Museum, Kimono; https://www.vam.ac.uk/articles/kimono . Facts paraphrased; no museum prose or images reproduced.

text: In Edo-period Japan, fine komon designs were made by applying dye-resisting paste through paper stencils. The Met’s fern-patterned summer kosode, dated late eighteenth to early nineteenth century, preserves this technique.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Robe (Kosode) with Ferns, 2001.428.43; https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/61838 . Object facts paraphrased.

text: The tiny repeated motifs of Edo komon cloth can look like an undecorated monochrome surface from a distance. A close view reveals the pattern: the Met’s late-Edo fern robe rewards proximity rather than a large silhouette.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Robe (Kosode) with Ferns, 2001.428.43; https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/61838 . Object facts paraphrased.

text: Edo komon cloth was developed for samurai formal garments and later adopted more widely. The Met’s late-eighteenth- to early-nineteenth-century example is a woman’s summer robe made from gauze-weave silk.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Robe (Kosode) with Ferns, 2001.428.43; https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/61838 . Object facts paraphrased.

text: An early-seventeenth-century Japanese kosode in the Met combines silk imported from China with decoration applied in Japan. The imported woven foundation was resist-dyed, then embroidered with shells and sea grasses.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Robe (Kosode) with Shells and Sea Grasses, 1992.253; https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/50688 . Object facts paraphrased.

text: The Met’s early-seventeenth-century Japanese shell-and-sea-grass kosode adds gold-leaf accents over pale-blue bands, emphasizing floral motifs already present in its woven silk. Weaving, dyeing, embroidery, and applied gold cooperate on one surface.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Robe (Kosode) with Shells and Sea Grasses, 1992.253; https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/50688 . Object facts paraphrased.

text: A late-Edo Japanese woman’s kosode at LACMA uses cotton fabric made in India and block-printed as sarasa. Its late-eighteenth- to mid-nineteenth-century date documents imported patterned cotton becoming a Japanese garment.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; Los Angeles County Museum of Art, M.2006.38.2; https://collections.lacma.org/object/133261 . Object facts paraphrased.

text: In Edo-period Japan, Kyoto-developed yūzen dyeing expanded the colors and designs available for kosode. Tokyo Metropolitan Library’s historical account ties the technique to a major mid-Edo shift in garment patterning.
provenance: Original factual paraphrase; Tokyo Metropolitan Library, Edo Tokyo Digital Museum, The Coming of Kosode Age; https://www.library.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/portals/0/edo/tokyo_library/english/fashion/page1-1.html . Facts paraphrased.
